samasa.vigraha: सर्वे च ते असुराः च, तान्
samasa.sense: the whole host of the asuras
cleansed of their sin by the stroke of her weapon

samasa.type: tatpuruṣa of the prādi kind (the prefix अति ‘exceedingly’ with an adjective)

morph.note: Present of प्र + √हि (svādi class, stem हिनो-): ‘you send forth’. After the r of the prefix प्र, the n of the stem becomes ṇ (हिनोषि → प्रहिणोषि).
Third person with the honorific भवती. The next clause turns to the direct second person (प्रहिणोषि): both address the Goddess.
Neuter of भस्मन् ‘ash’. With √कृ it is a predicative accusative: ‘make (them) ash’.

mantras.anvaya: (हे देवि) भवती दृष्ट्वा एव सर्वासुरान् भस्म किं न प्रकरोति, यत् अरिषु शस्त्रं प्रहिणोषि? ‘रिपवः अपि शस्त्रपूताः (सन्तः) लोकान् प्रयान्तु’ हि — इत्थं तेषु अपि ते मतिः अतिसाध्वी भवति।
mantras.anvaya_en: A question (किं न … प्रकरोति), whose occasion is the यत्-clause (‘that you hurl a weapon’). Line 3 gives the Goddess’s own wish as the answer; line 4 is the gods’ verdict on it.
mantras.lit: Why do you not make all the asuras ash merely by looking, that you hurl a weapon at the enemies? ‘Let even the enemies, purified by the weapon, go to the worlds’ — for thus is your thought, exceedingly kind even towards them.
mantras.tr: Why do you not burn all the asuras to ash with a single glance, but hurl your weapons at them instead? Because you would have even your enemies, made pure by your weapons, reach the higher worlds. So kind is your intent, even towards them.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Because’ renders हि; ‘the higher worlds’ interprets लोकान् ‘the worlds’, as 4.18 (दिवं प्रयान्तु) shows.

comm.t: The gods answer their own question. She could destroy the asuras by sight alone, but she uses weapons so that their touch may purify her enemies and send them to the higher worlds. Even her choice of weapon is an act of kindness.

The verse carries 4.18 further: death at the Goddess’s hand is read as purification (पूत), not only punishment. The tradition draws from it that her anger and her grace are one act seen from two sides.

samasa.literal: by the flashings of the mass of the sword’s light
samasa.sense: by the blinding flashes of her sword

samasa.literal: by the stream of lustre of the trident’s tip
samasa.sense: by the glare from the point of her trident

samasa.vigraha: इन्दोः खण्डम् इन्दुखण्डम्; अंशुमत् इन्दुखण्डम् अंशुमदिन्दुखण्डम्; तस्य योग्यम् अंशुमदिन्दुखण्डयोग्यम्; तत् च तत् आननम्
samasa.type: karmadhāraya; its first member is a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (…योग्य) built on a karmadhāraya (अंशुमदिन्दुखण्ड) that contains a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (इन्दुखण्ड)
samasa.literal: the face fit for a ray-bearing piece of the moon
samasa.sense: your face, like the radiant crescent moon
samasa.alt: अंशुमत् ‘ray-bearing’ is also a name of the sun; as a dvandva (अंशुमान् च इन्दुखण्डं च) the face would be ‘worthy of the sun and the crescent’. The verse needs an image that spares the eyes after the glare of the weapons, which points to the moon; so अंशुमत् is taken as its qualifier.

morph.note: Present participle of the curādi stem लोकय- with वि, gen. pl.: ‘of (them) gazing at’. It agrees with असुराणाम्; it is not an imperative, which would not fit the sentence.
Past participle of a verb of motion, active in sense: ‘(they) went (to)’. Feminine plural, to agree with दृशः.
Nominative plural of the root-noun दृश् (feminine), ‘eye’, ‘sight’.

mantras.anvaya: खड्गप्रभानिकरविस्फुरणैः उग्रैः तथा शूलाग्रकान्तिनिवहेन तव अंशुमदिन्दुखण्डयोग्याननं विलोकयताम् असुराणां दृशः यत् विलयं न आगताः, तत् एतत् (तव आननस्य दर्शनस्य फलम्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The यत्-clause carries the fact: the asuras’ eyes were not destroyed. तत् एतत् ‘that is this’ points to the participle phrase as its reason: they were gazing at your face.
mantras.lit: That, by the fierce flashings of the mass of the sword’s light and likewise by the stream of lustre from the trident’s point, the eyes of the asuras did not go to destruction, (they) gazing at your face fit for the radiant crescent of the moon — that is this.
mantras.tr: The blazing flashes of your sword and the flood of light from the point of your trident did not destroy the asuras’ eyes — because they were gazing at your face, like the radiant crescent of the moon.
mantras.tr_note: तत् एतत् (‘that is this’) points to the participle विलोकयताम् as the reason; English makes it ‘because’.

comm.t: Another wonder of the battle: the glare of her weapons should have blinded the asuras, but their eyes were not destroyed. The gods give the reason: they were looking at her face, which is like the moon.

The moon is the standing image of what cools and soothes; the verse sets it against the fierce light of sword and trident. The same face that terrifies in 4.13 here protects even her enemies, the theme of 4.18–21.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also likens her face to the moon: शरच्चन्द्रनिभानना (name 129), ‘whose face is like the autumn moon’. The image is shared devotional language; the works are separate.

samasa.sense: putting an end to the deeds of the wicked
samasa.alt: दुर्वृत्त is itself a bahuvrīhi, दुष्टं वृत्तं येषां ते, ‘those whose conduct is bad’.

samasa.vigraha: देवानां पराक्रमः देवपराक्रमः; हृतः देवपराक्रमः यैः तेषाम्
samasa.literal: of those by whom the gods’ valour was taken
samasa.sense: of the asuras who had stripped the gods of their power

morph.note: Agent noun of √हन् (suffix tṛc), ‘slayer’, here neuter to agree with वीर्यम्. Like other agent nouns it takes its object in the genitive (हृतदेवपराक्रमाणाम्).
Past participle of the denominative प्रकटय- ‘make evident’ (from the adjective प्रकट), feminine to agree with दया; त्वया is its agent.
The negative prefix with the gerundive विचिन्त्य (वि + √चिन्त्, curādi, + -य): ‘not to be conceived’.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) देवि, तव शीलं दुर्वृत्तवृत्तशमनम्; तथा एतत् रूपम् अविचिन्त्यम् अन्यैः अतुल्यं (च); वीर्यं च हृतदेवपराक्रमाणां हन्तृ; इत्थं त्वया वैरिषु अपि दया प्रकटिता एव।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three nominal sentences (on शील, रूप and वीर्य), then a passive verdict (दया … प्रकटिता) with त्वया as agent; इत्थम् sums up what 4.18–20 described.
mantras.lit: O Devī, your nature is the quelling of the conduct of the wicked; likewise this form is inconceivable and unequalled by others; and (your) valour is the slayer of those who had robbed the gods of their prowess; thus compassion has indeed been shown by you even towards enemies.
mantras.tr: O Devī, it is your nature to put an end to the ways of the wicked; your form is beyond thought, and none can equal it; your valour destroys those who robbed the gods of their might — and in this way you have shown compassion even to your enemies.

comm.t: The gods sum up the Goddess under three heads, her nature (शील), her form (रूप) and her valour (वीर्य), and draw the conclusion of 4.18–20: in this very way, by slaying them in battle, she has shown compassion even to her enemies.

The three heads echo the gods’ earlier question in 4.6 (रूपमचिन्त्यमेतत्, अतिवीर्यम्, चरितानि). The point traditionally drawn is that her severity is itself mercy: the act that protects the gods also purifies the asuras.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) calls the Goddess अव्याजकरुणामूर्तिः (name 992), ‘compassion embodied, without a pretext’. The Devī Māhātmya makes a related point by example: compassion shown to those who did nothing to earn it.
